why: Edward Elmer Smith, a food chemist who wrote space opera in his spare time, imagined more of the machinery of the later twentieth century than anyone else in the corpus. His Skylark and Lensman novels score on 163 separate ideas. Kimball Kinnison opens a door by fitting his eye to a retina scanner in Triplanetary (1948), 36 years before EyeDentify shipped the first ones. The Skylark of Space (1928) carries pocket wireless telephones and a link from one brain to another, and later books add driverless cars and three-dimensional telepresence. Few of his hits are exact, but there are more of them than anyone else's.

Godfrey Sweven was the pen name of John Macmillan Brown, a Scottish-born professor in New Zealand. Limanora, the Island of Progress (1903) tours a utopia run on applied science, and it scores on 81 ideas, the most of any single work: a tidal power station (the Rance, 1966), liquid air stored as grid energy (a plant near Manchester, 2018), a gas that puts crowds to sleep, implants that sharpen the senses, and screening of the whole population for disease.

In 1835 the New York Sun ran a series claiming that John Herschel had seen winged people on the Moon. Richard Adams Locke wrote it as a hoax, but in passing it accepts that lunar volcanoes could throw fragments of their craters beyond the Moon's pull, to fall on the Earth. In 1982 a meteorite found in Antarctica, Allan Hills 81005, was shown to be a piece of the Moon. The judges scored the match 0.875, and it came 148 years early, which makes it the single prediction worth the most points.

In Cyrano de Bergerac's comic moon voyage, published in 1657 after his death, the narrator rises in a machine ringed with rockets that fire one tier after another, each lit by a fuse from the tier below. That is a staged rocket, 287 years before Germany fired its four-stage Rheinbote in 1944. The same book gives the Moon's people books made for the ears, which play when wound up.

In "The Jameson Satellite" (Amazing Stories, 1931) a professor has his body put into orbit around the Earth after his death to preserve it, and the story dates the launch to 1958. Sputnik 1 went up on 4 October 1957, one year early, 26 years after the story was printed.

Simon Newcomb, the leading American astronomer of his day, wrote in 1906 that no combination of known substances, machinery and forces could make a practical machine to carry men long distances through the air. Within four years, airplanes were carrying people and mail across cities and countries. A check of all 82 skeptics the pipeline flagged confirmed that his was a real "never" that came true, and it was refuted the soonest.

By date of publication, Verne was the first author in the corpus to predict 61 ideas that later came true, more than anyone else. All Around the Moon (1870) alone has spacesuits, the point between Earth and Moon where their pulls cancel (where ISEE-3 was parked in 1978), and a second, tiny moon of the Earth (2006 RH120). Five Weeks in a Balloon (1863) burns hydrogen and oxygen for power, as the Centaur rocket stage did a century later.

The Achievements of Luther Trant (1910) follows a young psychologist who solves crimes with laboratory instruments, and nearly half of its 54 predictions came true at a judged 0.5 or closer, the best record of any author with 50 or more. Trant's blood-pressure lie detector was put to use by the Berkeley police in 1921, and the book's word-association tests and other methods of psychological detection followed.

Elam wrote three books of near-future space stories for young readers in the 1950s, and the details of the space age kept arriving after them: oxygen made from the Martian air (MOXIE, 2021), tourist hops into space (Blue Origin's first crewed flight, 2021), an inflatable room on a space station (BEAM, 2016) and the emergency drills of a crew sealing off a holed module (Mir, 1997). That averages 44.9 points a book.

Verne's books before 1900 score 338 points on 105 ideas, the most of any nineteenth-century writer. His moon travelers float weightless in their projectile, as Gagarin did in 1961; they wear spacesuits, pass the point where Earth's and the Moon's gravity cancel, and see a second small moon of the Earth. Five Weeks in a Balloon (1863) imagines hydrogen and oxygen as fuel and a searchlight carried aloft.

Smith's Skylark novels of 1928 to 1934 and the early Lensman books carry most of his points: telepresence, driverless cars, a link from brain to brain and machines that read thoughts and print them, each 70 years or more ahead, and 129 ideas in all from before 1946.

Leinster wrote for six decades; his books from 1946 on score 305 points on 134 ideas, the most of the postwar era. Med Service (1957) has a gas that puts a crowd to sleep, as Russian forces used in Moscow in 2002; If You Was a Moklin (1951) has private spaceships; The Last Space Ship (1949) has weapons that destroy objects in orbit, and Pariah Planet (1961) teaches people in their sleep.

T. Baron Russell's A Hundred Years Hence (1905) looked forward a century, and its 100 points on 32 ideas beat Wells's Anticipations among the forecasters: shared rental cars picked up on the street (Montpellier, 1971), high-speed trains (the TGV, 1981), machines that clean the house and the floor, and one that washes a person.

New Atlantis (1627) describes Salomon's House, a state research institute, and lists what its scientists can do: "helps" set to the ear that improve hearing (the Akouphone, 1900), towers half a mile high, new kinds of animals bred in the laboratory, and rain made to order.

Kipling's two stories of a world run by the Aerial Board of Control, "With the Night Mail" and "As Easy as A.B.C.", imagine the instruments of airline flying in detail: a recorder of the flight, a moving map in the cockpit, and zones where instruments and engines fail. They are collected in Actions and Reactions (1909) and A Diversity of Creatures (1917).

Wallace's stories of the 1950s put robots to work as nannies, waiters and companions, and The Man Who Was Six (1954) imagines immersive virtual reality 36 years before VPL sold the first headsets. Delay in Transit (1952) has a rewritable electronic page, which E Ink first showed in a shop in 1999.

Smith's heroes carry pocket wireless telephones in 1928, 55 years before the first commercial cellular call, choose films to watch on demand, talk mind to mind through a machine, and meet in three-dimensional projection.

Griffith, a Victorian journalist, filled his future-war novels with aircraft: helicopters and vertical-takeoff airships in The Angel of the Revolution (1893), high-speed trains in Olga Romanoff (1894), and a flying submarine in The World Peril of 1910 (1906).
Verne imagined hydrogen and oxygen as fuel in Five Weeks in a Balloon (1863), heat stored from one season to the next in Topsy-Turvy (1889), and an electric aircraft in Robur the Conqueror (1886).

Limanora's islanders sharpen and add to their senses with implants, put each other to sleep with a spray or a current, stun without killing, and screen everyone for disease, all ideas that came true from 1936 to 2004.

Smith armed his heroes with microwave weapons (a US Air Force source, 1988), cutting beams that slice metal (the first laser cutting machine, 1970), sleep gas and powered armor, the exoskeleton DARPA's BLEEX showed in 2004.

From the Earth to the Moon and All Around the Moon get the physics of the trip right more often than any other books: weightlessness, spacesuits, the point where Earth's and the Moon's gravity cancel, and a second small moon of the Earth.

The Purchase of the North Pole (1889) has astronomical cycles changing the Earth's climate, which Hays, Imbrie and Shackleton confirmed in 1976. Verne also imagined rivers diverted across a continent and the slow loss of a planet's air.

Leiber's stories of the 1950s put robots to work selling things: robot mannequins in The Green Millennium (1953), on sale from 2009, and a robot salesman in "A Bad Day for Sales" (1953). The Green Millennium also has paper clothing worn once and thrown away (1966).

Among the technology of society, Wells foresaw machines that count votes (Anticipations, 1901), a central register of every citizen (When the Sleeper Wakes, 1899) and a mathematical science of politics (The Discovery of the Future, 1902). The social and political predictions themselves are in tranche B.

The Time Machine (1895) treats time as a fourth dimension of space thirteen years before Minkowski's lecture, and other stories add synthetic diamonds (General Electric, 1957), clothing that changes color, and buildings put up by machine.

The Mahabharata reached its final form by about 400 CE, so every idea it shares with the modern world counts at the 500-year cap. It wins on breadth, not precision: 23 ideas, none judged closer than 0.5. A conch blast that leaves whole armies without strength (a ship drove off pirates with an acoustic device in 2005), a weapon that sends the foe to sleep, a poison neutralized by another poison (Calmette's antivenom, 1895), and yogic control of the breath and body. Lucian's True History, with its flight on borrowed wings and its eyes that can be taken out, is second.
